usage: everyday word for 'wow, cool!' when something is new or surprising in a good way
adverbial 신기하다 + 게도; opens a sentence: 신기하게도 비가 딱 그쳤어 = amazingly the rain stopped right then
polite -네요 of fresh discovery; mild wonder at something you just learned or saw
신기한 (modifier) + 거(것); 신기한 거 봤어 = I saw something cool
examples: 이 꽃 진짜 신기해.
This flower is really cool.
shortest 반말 form; just point and react, no object particle needed
한국 지하철은 환승이 잘 돼 있어서 신기해요.
The Korean subway transfers are so well-organized, it's amazing.
-아서 reason + 신기해요; everyday remark foreigners share with Korean friends
눈을 처음 봤을 때 너무 신기했어.
When I saw snow for the first time it was so amazing.
past 신기했어 recalling a first experience; object 눈을 marks what amazed you
nuance: 신기하다 is the go-to word for delighted, almost childlike wonder at something new, clever, or unexpected — a smart gadget, your first snow, a magic trick. The connotation is warm and positive. The Sino-Korean root is 神奇 (신기), literally 'divine + marvelous', so the feeling is that something is marvelously beyond the ordinary. The sharpest contrast is with 이상하다 ('weird/off'): both react to the unfamiliar, but 신기하다 is good-surprised ('cool!') while 이상하다 is bad-surprised ('something's wrong'). It also differs from 놀랍다 ('astonishing', more shock than charm). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like 'strange' — saying 신기하다 about a creepy noise sounds like you enjoyed it. As an adjective it never takes 를; you say 이게 신기해, not 이걸 신기해.

Writing the verbish 신기다 or conjugating 신기다 — the dictionary form keeps 하: 신기하다, 신기해요, 신기한.
Adding 를 as if it were a verb: 이걸 신기해(X). It is descriptive, so the thing that amazes you takes 이/가: 이게 신기해(O).

usage: for a view, music, or moment so beautiful you almost lose yourself
반말, said softly while taking something gorgeous in
황홀한 (modifier) + noun; classic for sunsets, night views, 야경
황홀하다 + -ㄹ 정도로 = so beautiful that...; 황홀할 정도로 아름다웠어
examples: 노을이 정말 황홀해요.
The sunset is truly mesmerizing.
simple subject + 황홀해요; 노을(sunset) is the textbook trigger
벚꽃 길을 걷는데 황홀하더라.
Walking the cherry blossom path, it was just breathtaking.
-더라 reporting a vivid first-hand impression to a friend
공연이 너무 황홀해서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어.
The show was so enchanting I lost track of time.
-아서 cause chained to the set phrase 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어
nuance: 황홀하다 describes beauty so intense it nearly sweeps you out of yourself — reserved for sunsets, night views, sublime music, a magical moment, never an everyday 'pretty'. The Sino-Korean 恍惚 (황홀) literally means 'dazed/entranced', so the word names the spellbound state of the viewer as much as the beauty itself, and it sounds literary and heightened. Contrast it with 아름답다 ('beautiful', the neutral aesthetic word) and 예쁘다 ('pretty', casual and small-scale): dropping 황홀하다 on a so-so cafe latte sounds theatrical. It also differs from 행복하다 ('happy'), which is general well-being, not being dazzled by beauty. The pitfall for English speakers is using it as a synonym for 'lovely/nice'; in Korean it implies near-overwhelm, so save it for genuinely stunning sights and pair it with 진짜/정말 or -할 정도로 for emphasis.

Confusing it with 행복하다 (general happiness) — 황홀하다 is specifically about being entranced by beauty or a sublime moment, not everyday contentment.
Applying it to a person's looks bluntly ('너 황홀해') — it sounds odd/over-the-top about a person; for that use 예쁘다/멋지다, and reserve 황홀하다 for scenes and experiences.

usage: the rush when you almost got hurt or look down from a height
반말 reaction right after a near-miss
past tense, retelling a scary moment that already passed
it's dizzying just to think about it
fixed phrase 생각만 해도 + 아찔하다 = I shudder to imagine
examples: 밑을 보니까 아찔해.
Looking down, I feel dizzy.
bare 반말; height-induced vertigo in the moment
차가 갑자기 끼어들어서 진짜 아찔했어요.
A car cut in suddenly and it was really heart-stopping.
-아서 cause + past; the near-accident-on-the-road use, extremely common
하마터면 지갑을 잃어버릴 뻔했어. 아찔해.
I almost lost my wallet. That was scary-close.
set frame 하마터면 …-ㄹ 뻔했어, then 아찔해 as the aftershock
nuance: 아찔하다 captures the dizzy, stomach-dropping jolt of a near-miss or a dangerous height — the physical wave of 'whew, that was close'. It is at once literal vertigo and the split-second emotional shock of almost-disaster, which is why Koreans say it constantly after close calls in traffic. It is an onomatopoeic/mimetic adjective (from 아찔, the lurch of light-headedness), so there is no 한자. The key contrast is with 무섭다 ('scary'), which is steady, ongoing fear, whereas 아찔하다 is one instantaneous lurch; and with 짜릿하다 ('thrilling'), which is the pleasant tingle of excitement. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'dizzy = 어지럽다': 어지럽다 is plain medical dizziness (low blood sugar, spinning room), while 아찔하다 adds the danger/shock element. It habitually pairs with 하마터면…뻔하다 and 생각만 해도.

usage: the cold shiver when something is eerie or menacing
반말, reacting to a horror scene or unsettling sight
past tense, retelling an eerie moment after the fact
섬뜩한 (modifier) + noun; common with 느낌, 분위기, 눈빛
examples: 그 그림 좀 섬뜩해.
That painting is kind of creepy.
short 반말 + softener 좀; reacting to an unsettling image
밤에 혼자 그 골목을 지나가는데 섬뜩했어.
Walking through that alley alone at night was creepy.
-는데 background + past; the lone-dark-alley scene
그 사람 눈빛이 진짜 섬뜩하더라.
That person's stare was really chilling.
-더라 reporting a vivid impression of someone; 눈빛(gaze) is a stock partner
nuance: 섬뜩하다 is the cold-spine, hair-raising creepiness of something eerie or sinister — a dark alley, an unsettling stare, a disturbing news story. It names the sudden chill that runs down your back, sharper and colder than the general fear of 무섭다. It is a native Korean mimetic word (from 섬뜩, the feel of a cold jolt), so there is no 한자. Compare it with three neighbors: 무섭다 ('scary', broad ongoing fear, even of exams); 소름 끼치다 ('to get goosebumps', very close and often interchangeable, focusing on the skin reaction); and 으스스하다 ('spooky/chilly', a milder ambient creepiness). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'creepy' loosely the way English does for a mildly off person ('he's a bit creepy'); in Korean that everyday 'off/sketchy' nuance is closer to 좀 이상하다, and 섬뜩하다 should be saved for a genuinely spine-chilling jolt. It pairs naturally with 눈빛, 분위기, 느낌, 사건.

usage: covers both an awkward mood and an upset, heavy stomach
to feel queasy in the stomach
fixed collocation; 속(insides) + 이 + 거북하다 = bloated/uneasy stomach
this feels awkward / my stomach's off
반말; meaning flips with context (people vs. 속이)
V-기 거북하다 pattern = uncomfortable/awkward to do something
examples: 속이 좀 거북해.
My stomach feels a bit off.
the core stomach use; 속이 + 거북해, softened with 좀
과식했더니 속이 거북해요.
I overate, so my stomach feels queasy.
-았더니 (I did X and as a result) + the 속이 거북하다 collocation
솔직히 그 질문은 대답하기 거북했어요.
Honestly, that question was awkward to answer.
V-기 거북하다 (대답하기 거북하다) for a question you'd rather not field
nuance: 거북하다 has two everyday lives: a queasy, heavy, ill-sitting stomach (속이 거북하다) and an awkward, uneasy social feeling (분위기가 거북하다, 마주치기 거북하다). Both share the core image of something not sitting right — physically or emotionally. The sharpest contrast is with 불편하다: 불편하다 covers broad 'inconvenient/uncomfortable', including practical inconvenience (불편한 의자 = an uncomfortable chair, 교통이 불편하다 = bad transit), whereas 거북하다 is the more inward, visceral 'this doesn't sit well with me' and is the natural word for an upset stomach. For a hard chair or bad transit you must use 불편하다, not 거북하다. It also overlaps with 어색하다 ('awkward, unfamiliar between people'), but 거북하다 adds a note of mild distaste or discomfort, not just unfamiliarity. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping all of 'uncomfortable' onto one word; remember 거북하다 for queasy stomachs and for situations you find off-putting, and 불편하다 for physical/practical discomfort.

Using it for first-meeting shyness ('I felt 거북해 meeting new people') — pure unfamiliar awkwardness is 어색하다; 거북하다 implies it actively bothers you.

usage: to feel let down by someone's coldness
soft resentment when someone you care about is unkind or distant
반말, gentle reproach to a close person
-더라 recalling a moment you personally felt slighted
야속한 (modifier) + noun; mild blame, not strong condemnation
examples: 너 진짜 야속해.
You're really being cold.
bare 반말 reproach said straight to the person who let you down
힘들 때 연락 한 번 없어서 좀 야속했어.
You didn't reach out once when I was struggling, it felt cold.
-아서 reason + softener 좀; classic complaint toward a friend
날씨까지 야속하게 비가 오네요.
Even the weather is being cruel — it's raining.
playful extension to fate/circumstance with 야속하게 + 까지
nuance: 야속하다 is the soft, wounded resentment you feel when someone close lets you down or seems cold — less anger than quiet hurt. It carries an implicit 'I expected warmth from you and didn't get it', so there is affection tucked underneath the complaint, and it is most natural toward family, close friends, a partner, or even personified fate/weather. The nearest synonym is 섭섭하다 ('hurt/let down'), and the dividing line matters: 섭섭하다 is the broad ache of disappointment ('I'm sad you forgot my birthday'), while 야속하다 specifically blames the other side's apparent heartlessness ('how could you be so cold to me'). It is gentler and more inward than 매정하다 ('cold-hearted', a flatter description of someone) and far softer than 화나다 ('angry'). The English-speaker pitfall is reading it as real anger or using it about strangers and institutions; with strangers there is no prior warmth to betray, so it rings false — use 차갑다/매정하다 instead, and save 야속하다 for people (or fate) you feel close enough to gently reproach.

usage: the cozy warmth of a homey scene or close relationship
정겨운 (ㅂ-irregular modifier) + noun; 정겹 + 은 → 정겨운
adverb form; 정겹게 인사하다 = greet warmly
examples: 우리 동네는 참 정겨워.
My neighborhood is really cozy and warm.
shortest 반말; note the ㅂ-irregular 정겹다 → 정겨워, not 정겹어
할머니 댁은 늘 정겨운 냄새가 나.
Grandma's house always has a cozy, homey smell.
정겨운 (modifier) + 냄새; the ㅂ-irregular -은 form 정겨운
오랜만에 만났는데 정겹게 안아줬어요.
We hadn't met in ages and they hugged me warmly.
정겹게 (adverb) + 안아주다; warmth expressed through an action
nuance: 정겹다 carries the uniquely Korean feeling of 정(情) — deep, accumulated affectionate warmth between people — so it names the cozy, homey heart you get from a traditional market, an old neighborhood, or a close-knit gathering. The headword is 정(情, 'affection/bond') + 겹다 ('to be full of / overflowing with'), so it literally means 'brimming with 정'. It is about human warmth and connection, not mere physical comfort or temperature, which sets it apart from 따뜻하다 ('warm') — 따뜻하다 can be literal heat or a warm personality, while 정겹다 is specifically that 정-soaked, nostalgic homeyness, and it leans gentle and a touch literary. It also differs from 포근하다 ('soft, snug, cozy'), which is about physical/emotional softness rather than the people-bond of 정. Grammatically the trap is huge: 정겹다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so it becomes 정겨워(요), 정겨운, 정겨우니까 — never the regular 정겹어요/정겹은. English speakers also over-apply it to cute objects; it is about heartfelt human warmth, not cuteness (그건 귀여워, not 정겨워).

usage: the aching fondness of longing or cherished love
반말, reacting to a touching story or memory
애틋한 (modifier) + 사이; common for couples or family
애틋한 + 마음; the set phrase for deep affectionate feeling
examples: 둘이 진짜 애틋해.
The two of them are so tenderly fond of each other.
short 반말 about a couple's bond; subject + 애틋해
멀리 떨어져 있으니까 더 애틋해요.
Being far apart makes the feeling even more tender.
-니까 reason + 더; distance intensifying tenderness, a core context
부모님 사진을 보면 애틋한 마음이 들어요.
Looking at my parents' photo brings a tender, longing feeling.
애틋한 마음 + 들다 — feelings 'arise' (들다), not 'come'
nuance: 애틋하다 is a tender, bittersweet fondness — the ache of cherishing someone you miss or love deeply, usually tinged with longing, distance, or the knowledge that the moment is precious and fragile. It is gentler and far more wistful than plain 좋아하다/사랑하다, adding a thread of melancholy, which is why it suits first loves, family far away, or a bond you hold close. The nearest neighbor is 애절하다 ('sorrowfully yearning'), but 애절하다 is more openly sad/desperate, while 애틋하다 keeps a warm, cherishing softness under the ache. It also contrasts with 안타깝다 ('it's a pity / I feel for their misfortune'): 안타깝다 is sympathy for an unfortunate situation, whereas 애틋하다 centers on tender longing toward a person or memory. The English-speaker pitfall is using it for casual liking the way 'fond of pizza' works in English — 애틋하다 is reserved for deep, bittersweet, person-directed tenderness, so for light liking use 좋아하다. A grammar note: feelings here arise with 들다 (마음이 들다), and the verb-ified 애틋해지다 means 'to grow tender'.

Feelings here arise with 들다 (마음이 들다), and the verb-ified 애틋해지다 means 'to grow tender'.
The English-speaker pitfall is using it for casual liking the way 'fond of pizza' works in English — 애틋하다 is reserved for deep, bittersweet, person-directed tenderness, so for light liking use 좋아하다.

mistakes: Using it for casual liking ('I'm 애틋해 about coffee') — 애틋하다 is deep, bittersweet tenderness toward a person or memory; light liking is 좋아하다.
Confusing it with 안타깝다 — 안타깝다 is pity for someone's misfortune, while 애틋하다 centers on tender, longing affection.
Saying 애틋한 마음이 와요 — feelings arise with 들다, so it is 애틋한 마음이 들어요, not 오다.

usage: for blurry distant memories or a dreamy, faint impression
아련한 (modifier) + 추억; the single most common partner noun
adverb; 아련하게 떠오르다/생각나다 = come faintly to mind
examples: 어릴 때 기억이 좀 아련해.
My childhood memories are kind of hazy.
short 반말; 기억(memory) as subject, softened with 좀
그 노래를 들으면 옛날 생각이 아련하게 나.
When I hear that song, old memories come back faintly.
아련하게 (adverb) + 생각이 나다 — the memory-surfacing collocation
사진 속 풍경이 아련해서 더 그리웠어요.
The scenery in the photo was hazy, making me miss it more.
-아서 linking 아련하다 to 그립다, the longing it triggers
nuance: 아련하다 describes something faint and hazy — above all distant memories that blur at the edges, leaving a soft, wistful longing behind. It fuses 'dim/indistinct' with gentle nostalgia, so in practice it almost always pairs with 추억(memories), 기억, or 생각, and with the adverb 아련하게 + 떠오르다/생각나다. The crucial contrast is with 흐릿하다 ('blurry/unclear'): 흐릿하다 is plain physical fuzziness — out-of-focus eyesight, a smudged photo, dim letters — with no emotion, while 아련하다 is dreamier and carries that bittersweet pull of the past. It also brushes against 어렴풋하다 ('vague, only faintly recalled'), which is closer to a neutral 'I can barely remember', whereas 아련하다 adds the warm, longing color. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it onto 'blurry/hazy vision' or any literal fuzz; if your eyes are blurry or a window is foggy, that is 흐릿하다/뿌옇다, not 아련하다. Reserve 아련하다 for faded, emotionally tinged memories, not clear or recent events.

usage: the chest-swelling satisfaction after an accomplishment
반말, the warm glow after doing something well
past tense, recalling a satisfying moment
examples: 오늘 운동 다 해서 뿌듯해.
I got through my whole workout today, so I feel fulfilled.
-아서 reason + 뿌듯해; the small-daily-win use, very common
드디어 한국어로 주문에 성공해서 너무 뿌듯했어요.
I finally managed to order in Korean, I felt so proud.
강조 너무 + past; a relatable learner win in Korea
방 청소를 다 하고 나니까 뿌듯해.
After finishing cleaning my room, I feel fulfilled.
-고 나니까 (after doing X, then I felt…) leading into 뿌듯해
nuance: 뿌듯하다 is the warm, chest-swelling pride and fulfillment you feel after accomplishing something — finishing a task, hitting a goal, even doing a small thing well. It is inward, modest satisfaction (the chest literally feeling 'full'), not bragging, so it shows up constantly in everyday self-talk. The native word comes from the mimetic sense of being filled to the brim. The key contrast is with 자랑스럽다 ('proud of'): 자랑스럽다 is typically outward and directed at a person or achievement you want to show off — 아들이 자랑스러워(I'm proud of my son), 한국인인 게 자랑스럽다 — and can imply boasting, while 뿌듯하다 is the quiet inner glow you feel for yourself and rarely takes an external object. It also differs from 만족하다 ('to be satisfied'), which is cooler and more evaluative ('the result meets my standard') versus the heart-warm emotion of 뿌듯하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 뿌듯하다 to mean 'proud of someone else' the way English 'proud' covers both; for that you generally want 자랑스럽다. Watch the spelling too: it is the tense ㅃ, 뿌듯하다, not 부듯하다.

usage: the bashful awkwardness after a small misstep or being caught
adverb; 겸연쩍게 웃다 = laugh awkwardly (the signature collocation)
겸연쩍은 (modifier) + noun; common with 표정, 미소
examples: 이름을 잘못 불러서 겸연쩍었어.
I called the wrong name, so I felt sheepish.
-아서 cause + past; a minor social slip-up, the prototypical trigger
칭찬을 받으니까 겸연쩍게 웃었어.
When I got complimented I laughed sheepishly.
겸연쩍게 (adverb) + 웃다; bashful reaction to praise
혼자 김칫국 마신 게 좀 겸연쩍더라.
Getting my hopes up for nothing felt a bit embarrassing.
-더라 + the idiom 김칫국(을) 마시다 (count chickens too early)
nuance: 겸연쩍다 is that mild, sheepish embarrassment when you have made a small slip or feel awkwardly self-conscious — the apologetic, bashful smile after being caught or praised. The -쩍다 ending is a productive suffix meaning 'giving the feeling of' (compare 멋쩍다, 객쩍다, 수상쩍다), and the 겸연(慊然) root adds a shade of feeling slightly ill-at-ease and apologetic. The contrast that matters most is with 창피하다 ('embarrassed/ashamed'), which is full, sometimes face-burning embarrassment over something genuinely mortifying, while 겸연쩍다 is light and bashful, often with a guilty/apologetic tinge. It overlaps heavily with 멋쩍다 ('awkward, at a loss for how to react'), the difference being that 멋쩍다 leans toward 'I don't know how to act' whereas 겸연쩍다 leans toward 'I feel a bit guilty/apologetic'. It is milder still than 부끄럽다 ('shy/ashamed'). The English-speaker pitfall is using it for deep shame or serious embarrassment; in Korean that is 창피하다. Its signature collocation is 겸연쩍게 웃다, the awkward little laugh.

english: having a clear conscience, upright, unashamed
usage: to be upright / have a clear conscience
confident you've done nothing wrong, nothing to hide
반말, standing by what you did
adverb; 떳떳하게 살다 = live honestly, head held high
to feel guilty / unable to hold one's head up
negative form for a guilty conscience
examples: 난 잘못한 게 없으니까 떳떳해.
I didn't do anything wrong, so my conscience is clear.
-니까 reason + 떳떳해; standing your ground in 반말
떳떳하게 일해서 번 돈이에요.
It's money I earned through honest work.
떳떳하게 (adverb) + 일하다; the 'earned honestly' collocation
거짓말한 게 있어서 떳떳하지 못했어요.
I had told a lie, so I couldn't feel at ease.
negative 떳떳하지 못하다 expressing a guilty conscience
nuance: 떳떳하다 means having a clear conscience — being able to hold your head up because you have done nothing shameful or dishonest. It is about moral confidence and integrity, and it lives especially in the adverb 떳떳하게 ('openly, honestly') and the negative 떳떳하지 못하다 ('to feel guilty, unable to look others in the eye'). It is a native Korean word (no 한자), built on the mimetic 떳떳 of standing firm and aboveboard. The sharpest contrast is with 당당하다: both translate loosely as 'confident', but 당당하다 is about bold, self-assured bearing and presence (어깨를 펴고 당당하게 = standing tall and confident) regardless of right or wrong, while 떳떳하다 specifically grounds that confidence in a clean conscience and having nothing to hide. It is not the same as 자신 있다 ('to be confident in one's ability') either — that is about competence, not morality. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'proud' or 'confident'; 떳떳하다 is narrower, meaning 'in the moral clear'. Watch the spelling: doubled ㄸ and patchim ㅅ, 떳떳하다, and keep the 하 — 떳떳해요, 떳떳하게.
